## What DeFi Lending Is and How It Works

**DeFi lending** lets users borrow and lend crypto assets directly through smart contracts, without banks, exchanges, or brokerages in between. **DeFi lending and borrowing platform development** means building the product that gives users access to these tools. Blockchain-based smart contracts enable activities such as lending/borrowing, cryptocurrency trading, and interest earned in savings-like accounts. One of the most distinctive features of DeFi is that it’s free from centralized management, which typically controls transactions.

To see why this model matters, look at how lending got here. Lending is as old as money itself, and over time traditional collective and investment property loans gave way to the peer-to-peer (P2P) model.

A **distinctive** **feature of P2P** is that it lets borrowers and lenders collaborate through an online P2P platform instead of applying to banks as traditional intermediaries. As a result, both parties benefit. Borrowers can quickly access the required funds without banking bureaucracy, and investors can access direct funding with better terms and a higher interest rate.

The Internet has significantly changed the scope and possibilities of P2P lending relationships: lending companies have had an opportunity to create online marketplaces that can serve as mediators during borrowers' and lenders' collaboration. Transactions are based on borrowers' credit histories and the underlying assets (if any) that support the loan.

### How a DeFi lending transaction runs

These systems function as follows:

* To launch the process, the borrower puts up the crypto assets as collateral.
* The platform offers loans based on [automated smart contracts use](https://www.cleveroad.com/blog/smart-contracts-blockchain/).
* Borrowers pay a specific interest rate, and lenders receive that interest.

This flow depends on three parameters that the protocol checks around the clock. A price oracle, such as Chainlink, feeds the current market value of the collateral into the smart contract. The collateralization ratio compares that value with the size of the loan, and each asset has a liquidation threshold, for example, 80% loan-to-value. Once a price drop pushes a position past the threshold, the liquidation engine lets third-party liquidators repay part of the debt and take the collateral at a discount, so lenders get their funds back.

## Features That a DeFi Lending Platform Should Support

When planning decentralized finance platform development, one of the first things you should do is to create a feature list for an upcoming platform. We’ll cover the basic features you should include in your ideal DeFi solution with the help of DeFi lending/borrowing platform development services.

Most of these features run on-chain, since decentralization is the core idea behind [Web 3.0 development](https://www.cleveroad.com/blog/web3-development/).

### Borrowing and lending

**Borrowing and lending** are necessary to manage collateral ratios, cryptocurrency assets, and supply and demand. Keep in mind that lending and borrowing are the main reasons customers join your platform, so you must ensure they function properly.

### Flash loans

**Flash loans** let users borrow funds with no collateral, as long as they repay the loan within the same blockchain transaction. Traders use them for arbitrage and other smart contract-automated operations.

### Rate switching

The rate switching feature lets borrowers move a loan between stable and variable interest rates. A variable rate follows pool utilization and changes with liquidity demand, while a stable rate keeps payments predictable. Your users can lock in a stable rate before a demand spike and switch back to variable when the market calms down.

### Margin trading

Margin trading lets traders open positions larger than their own capital by borrowing funds against collateral. With 3x leverage, for example, a $1,000 deposit controls a $3,000 position, so even a small price move brings a noticeable profit or loss. To support it, your platform needs real-time price oracles and an automated liquidation engine that closes risky positions before they turn into bad debt.

### DeFi wallets

**DeFi wallets** should be provided to properly deposit customers’ assets. You may need several, or a branded crypto wallet that adds value for DeFi users. Moreover, it should support a variety of tokens and stablecoins.

### Fiat gateway

**The fiat gateway** feature enables users to exchange fiat money for traditional crypto (usually called fiat currencies, while others are called non-fiat ones). It also lets newbies start using the platform even without any cryptocurrency assets.

### Smart contract

**Smart contracts** ensure full decentralization of the DeFi system. They act as automated digital mediators, handling the flow of funds, transactions, and calculations on the platform, so careful [smart contract development](https://www.cleveroad.com/blog/smart-contracts-blockchain/) determines how reliably the whole system runs.

### Liquidity pool

A liquidity pool holds the funds that lenders deposit into a smart contract, and borrowers take loans directly from this shared reserve. The size of the pool limits how much your platform can lend at any moment, so low liquidity leads to failed loan requests and sharp rate jumps. To keep the pool healthy, your platform should track the utilization rate in real time and adjust interest rates as demand changes.

### Investment rewards

Investment rewards motivate lenders to deposit funds on your platform and keep them there longer. Beyond the base interest, many DeFi lending platforms pay governance tokens or loyalty bonuses for long-term deposits. A clear reward model helps you grow the liquidity pool faster, and vesting periods with reward caps protect your token from sudden sell-offs.

### Governance

Governance gives token holders the right to propose and vote on platform changes, such as adding new assets or updating interest rate models. Key decisions move from the core team to the community, building trust among users who keep their funds on the platform. In practice, smart contracts count votes by token weight and hold approved upgrades behind a time lock before they go live.

### User dashboard

The user dashboard is the control center where lenders and borrowers manage their positions. It should show deposited and borrowed amounts, current interest rates, earned rewards, and the health factor of each loan in a clear format. When users can see their earnings and liquidation risk at a glance, they act faster and trust the platform more, and that keeps them coming back.

Once the core is in place, you can extend the platform with yield swaps, credit delegation, staking, and isolated lending markets. A DeFi lending/borrowing platform development company can help you define which advanced features fit your product scope.

## What Regulation Applies to DeFi Lending

DeFi lending regulation depends on where your users are and who controls their assets, and in the European Union the answer is less obvious than it looks. The main EU framework is the Markets in Crypto-Assets Regulation (MiCA), fully applicable since December 2024. It sets the rules for crypto-asset issuers and Crypto-Asset Service Providers (CASPs), but lending sits in a separate category. Check this before you fix the architecture, since it shapes your custody model, risk disclosures, onboarding flow, and interface copy.

### Crypto lending sits outside MiCA

MiCA leaves the lending and borrowing of crypto-assets out of its scope, and Recital 94 of the regulation states this directly, deferring any rules for these activities to a later assessment. For your product, this has two practical consequences. A CASP license gives lending operations no legal cover of its own, and the MiCA safeguards for client asset protection stop at the funds users place in lending programs.

The [European Securities and Markets Authority](https://www.esma.europa.eu/esmas-activities/digital-finance-and-innovation/markets-crypto-assets-regulation-mica) (ESMA) collects its MiCA guidance and supervisory statements in one place. In its [June 2026 Q&A on crypto-asset lending](https://www.esma.europa.eu/publications-data/questions-answers/2883), ESMA confirmed that CASPs offering lending still carry MiCA's general duties: fair and non-misleading communication, express client consent before using their assets, and disclosure of significant risks.

### What that means for your product copy

ESMA separately warns about the risk of misleading users when a licensed provider offers regulated and unregulated services side by side. A user who sees a CASP license on your homepage can easily assume it covers every product in the app, including the lending pool.

The practical conclusion is that your interface and marketing must separate the two types of services explicitly. Treat it as a product requirement for your design team from the first wireframe: separate onboarding screens, clear labels on lending products, distinct terms of use, and separate balance views for regulated and lending assets.

### Risks you have to disclose

ESMA names three risks of crypto lending directly, and your platform has to explain each of them to users before they commit funds:

* **Counterparty risk**: the borrower or the provider fails to return the assets.
* **Collateral shortfall**: the collateral loses value faster than the protocol can liquidate it.
* **Loss of access**: users lose access to lent assets if the provider collapses.

You close most of these risks in the architecture rather than in the terms of service. Liquidation parameters set with a safety margin, a manipulation-resistant oracle setup with fallback feeds, and a reserve fund for bad debt together decide how much of the disclosed risk actually reaches your users.

### Jurisdiction decides the model

The same smart contracts can require very different product packaging depending on the market you launch in. In some jurisdictions, a fully non-custodial interface where users sign every transaction from their own wallets fits the rules, while in others the same service requires a licensed operator with **Know Your Customer (KYC) checks**, custody rules, and reporting duties.

That is why you should fix the list of target jurisdictions before the architecture, not after it. Custody, onboarding, and front-end access controls all follow from that choice, and changing them after launch costs far more than planning them upfront. Confirm the final model with legal counsel in each target market.

DeFi lending protocols compared: Aave, Compound III, Morpho

| Protocol | Lending model | Key features | Best fit |
| Aave | Shared liquidity pools where all lenders and borrowers use the same reserves | Flash loans that borrowers repay within one transaction, isolation mode for riskier assets | Platforms that need deep liquidity and a wide list of supported assets |

Frequently Asked Questions

What is a DeFi lending platform?

A DeFi lending platform is a web or mobile app where users lend and borrow crypto assets through smart contracts instead of a bank. Borrowers lock collateral, such as ETH, and lenders earn interest from a shared liquidity pool, with protocols like Aave or Morpho running the logic on-chain.

What are the benefits of a DeFi lending platform?

A DeFi lending platform connects lenders and borrowers directly through smart contracts, which cuts intermediary fees and lets lenders earn interest on deposits. Borrowers get funds against crypto collateral without a credit check, every transaction stays visible on-chain, and users keep their assets in their own wallets. Composability adds one more advantage: your platform can plug into existing protocols such as Aave or Morpho for liquidity instead of building it from zero.

* Select a proper cooperation model
* Decide the best region for collaboration
* Evaluate company’s tech expertise

Is DeFi lending regulated?

Partly. In the EU, MiCA leaves crypto-asset lending and borrowing out of scope (Recital 94), so a CASP license does not cover these services. Still, ESMA's June 2026 Q&A requires CASPs that offer lending to disclose counterparty, collateral, and insolvency risks. They also have to keep regulated and unregulated services clearly separated for users.
